tool.name: YAML
tool.tagline: The indentation-based data format behind most configuration files
tool.description: YAML is a human-friendly data serialization format used for Kubernetes manifests, CI pipelines, Docker Compose, Ansible and countless app configs. Learn its few structures, its string and typing rules and its traps, and every YAML-configured tool becomes easier to read and debug.

glossary.def: Writing a YAML list or mapping on one line with brackets, like [80, 443] or {cpu: 1, memory: 2}. It means exactly the same as the indented, one-item-per-line block style.
YAML's usual layout: one item or key per line, with indentation showing what belongs inside what.
A single YAML value written without quotes. YAML guesses its type from how it looks, so 42 becomes a number and true a boolean.
The - or + after | or > in YAML multi-line text: - removes the final line break, + keeps every trailing line break, and neither keeps exactly one.
A digit after | or > (like |2) telling YAML how far the multi-line text is indented, needed when its first line starts with spaces.
A label, written &name, that marks a piece of a YAML file so an alias (*name) can reuse it later in the same document.
In YAML, *name: a reference that reuses the piece of the file marked earlier with the anchor &name, so you write it only once.
In YAML, the special key << (the merge key), which copies the keys of another mapping, usually an alias, into this one; keys written next to it win. A YAML 1.1 feature many parsers still support.
In YAML, block means written over several lines with indentation (block style, block scalars), as opposed to the one-line flow style with brackets.
One complete piece of YAML data. A file can hold several, separated by lines containing just ---.
Everything a YAML parser reads in one go, such as a whole file, which may contain several YAML documents.
A line containing just --- (start of a YAML document) or ... (end of one).
The YAML trap where the country code NO is read as the boolean false by parsers following the older YAML 1.1 rules. Quoting it ("NO") fixes it.
Counting in base 60, as clocks do. YAML 1.1 reads values like 1:30 as base-60 numbers (90), which surprises people who meant a time.
A YAML-reading function that only builds plain data (text, numbers, lists, mappings) and refuses instructions to create other kinds of objects, so a file can't make it run code.
A small, malicious YAML file whose aliases refer to aliases again and again, so it expands to billions of items and exhausts the memory of whatever reads it.
A YAML library that remembers comments, key order and formatting when it reads a file, so a program can change one value and write the file back almost untouched.
The most widely used YAML library for Python (import yaml). It follows the older YAML 1.1 rules.
A Python YAML library that follows YAML 1.2 and can keep comments and formatting when it edits a file.
The simplest YAML rule set for guessing types: every single value is text. Nothing is ever turned into a number or boolean.
The step where a YAML parser decides the type of each value that has no explicit tag, following the rules of a schema.
The YAML spec's name for the parsed structure of a document: values, lists and mappings connected together, each with a type tag.
A helper program that code editors use to check YAML files as you type, show errors and suggest keys, based on a schema for the file.
A public online catalogue of schemas for common configuration files, which editors use to check files automatically by their name.
Writing a number as a value times a power of ten, like 1e3 for 1000 or 2.5e-3 for 0.0025.
In YAML, a label starting with ! or !! written before a value to state its type, like !!str 123 (the text 123). Tools also invent their own, such as !Ref.
In YAML libraries, the code that reads YAML text and builds data from it, such as yaml.safe_load in Python.
A short YAML document between --- lines at the very top of a Markdown or other text file, holding details about the file such as its title and date.
Multi-line text in YAML, started with | (keep line breaks) or > (join lines) after the key; the text is the indented lines below, with no quotes needed.

concepts.name: Mappings, sequences and indentation
concepts.summary: YAML stores data as name: value pairs (mappings) and - item lists (sequences), nested by indenting with spaces.
concepts.why: Almost every YAML file you'll meet, from an app's settings to the steps of an automated build, is these two structures nested inside each other.
concepts.body:
Many programs read their settings from a text file you can open and edit by hand, a **configuration file**. **YAML** is one of the most popular formats for writing them. It's designed to look like notes you'd jot down yourself: names, values and indented lists, with very little punctuation.

Every YAML file is built from three kinds of pieces. A **mapping** is a set of named values, like a form with a label next to each answer. A **sequence** is an ordered list. A **scalar** is one single value: a piece of text, a number, true or false, or "nothing".

A mapping writes each entry as `name: value`, one per line. YAML calls the name a **key**, and the two together a **key-value pair**. The space after the colon is required: `name:value` without the space is just one piece of text, not a pair.

A sequence writes each item on its own line, after `- ` (a dash and a space).

**Indentation**, the spaces at the start of a line, shows what belongs inside what. A line indented further than the line above it belongs to that line, the way sub-points sit under a heading in an outline. Use **spaces only**: the character the Tab key types isn't allowed for indentation. How many spaces is up to you (two is usual), but entries at the same level must line up exactly.

A list that is the value of a key may be indented, or start at the same position as the key; both of these mean the same:

```yaml
steps:
  - build
  - test
steps2:
- build
- test
```

`#` starts a **comment**: a note for human readers that runs to the end of the line and is ignored by programs. When it follows a value, put a space before the `#`.

A program that reads YAML text and turns it into data is called a YAML **parser**. Keys within one mapping must be unique. Their order carries no meaning in the data, although most parsers keep it.
concepts.code:
# a typical configuration file
name: web-app
version: 3
replicas: 2            # comments start with #
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
owner:
  team: platform
  email: platform@example.com
env:
- name: LOG_LEVEL      # a sequence whose items are mappings
  value: info
- name: REGION
  value: eu-west-1

# The same data written in JSON, another data format (next lessons):
# {"name": "web-app", "version": 3, "replicas": 2, "ports": [80, 443],
#  "owner": {"team": "platform", "email": "platform@example.com"},
#  "env": [{"name": "LOG_LEVEL", "value": "info"}, {"name": "REGION", "value": "eu-west-1"}]}
takeaways: `name: value` lines form mappings; `- item` lines form sequences
Indent with spaces only; entries at the same level must line up
A space is required after the colon and after the dash
pitfalls: Indenting with a tab character, which YAML rejects even when it looks lined up in your editor.

quiz.q: How is the line image:nginx read inside a mapping?
options: As the single piece of text image:nginx
As key image with value nginx
quiz.explain: Without a space after the colon it isn't a key-value separator, so the whole line is one text value.

quiz.q: Two keys under the same parent are indented by 2 and 3 spaces. What's wrong?
options: Entries at the same level must line up exactly
quiz.explain: You may choose the amount of indentation, but siblings must start at exactly the same column.

concepts.name: Scalars: strings, numbers, booleans, null
concepts.summary: YAML guesses each unquoted value's type: 42 is a whole number, 3.5 a decimal, true a yes/no value, null means nothing, and the rest is text.
concepts.why: Knowing how YAML guesses types stops values silently turning into the wrong kind of value in the program that reads them.
concepts.body:
Programs treat different kinds of values differently: they can add up numbers but not words. So when a parser reads a scalar, it decides which kind of value, or **data type**, it is. For a value written without quotes (a **plain scalar**), it decides by how the value looks.

The types YAML recognises, under the YAML 1.2 rules:

- **Integers**, whole numbers: `42`, `-7`. Technical settings sometimes use other number bases: `0o17` is base 8 (octal) and `0x1F` base 16 (hexadecimal).
- **Floats** (short for floating-point numbers), numbers with a decimal point: `3.14`, `1e3` (**scientific notation**, here 1 times 10³ = 1000), and the special values `.inf` (infinity) and `.nan` (**NaN**, "not a number").
- **Booleans**, the two values of a yes/no switch: `true` and `false` (also `True`, `TRUE`).
- **Null**, meaning "no value at all": `null`, `~`, or nothing after the colon.
- Everything else is a **string**, a piece of text: `hello world`, `eu-west-1`, `v1.2.3`.

Quotes force a string: `"42"` and `'true'` are text, not a number and a boolean. Most strings need no quotes, but some do (see the next section): those that look like another type, those that start with a character YAML uses for something else, such as `*`, `&`, `!`, `{`, `[`, `@` or `%`, and those that contain `: ` or ` #`.

Dates such as `2026-10-17` are a special case. Parsers that follow the older YAML 1.1 rules, including **PyYAML** (the most used YAML reader for the Python language), turn them into dates; YAML 1.2 keeps them as strings. Quote dates if the type matters.

A key with nothing after the colon has the value **null**, not an empty string. Write `""` for an empty string.

Plain strings can't be spread over several lines in a readable way; long text has its own notation, covered in the next section.
concepts.code:
count: 42              # integer
ratio: 0.75            # float
big: 1e6               # float 1000000.0 (a string in YAML 1.1 parsers)
enabled: true          # boolean
nothing: ~             # null
empty:                 # null as well, not ""
blank: ""              # empty string
version: "3.10"        # string; unquoted 3.10 would be the float 3.1
zip: "01234"           # string; keeps the leading zero
region: eu-west-1      # string
mode: 0o644            # octal (base 8): the integer 420 (YAML 1.1 parsers want 0644)
takeaways: Unquoted values get a type from how they look: integer, float, boolean, null or string
Quote a value to force a string, e.g. version: "3.10"
An empty value is null, not an empty string
pitfalls: Writing python_version: 3.10, which is read as the decimal number 3.1.

quiz.q: What is the value of key in key: (nothing after the colon)?
quiz.explain: A missing value counts as empty, and YAML reads an empty value as null.

quiz.q: Which line keeps the leading zero of 007?
quiz.explain: Quotes make it a string; unquoted, 007 is read as a number and the zeros disappear.

concepts.name: Flow style, and JSON inside YAML
concepts.summary: Write short lists and mappings on one line with [a, b] and {k: v}, and know that almost any JSON file is already valid YAML.
concepts.why: Short lists read better on one line, and knowing JSON is valid YAML helps when tools mix the two.
concepts.body:
So far you've written YAML in **block style**: one entry per line, with indentation. YAML also has a compact, one-line **flow style**:

- a flow sequence: `[80, 443]`;
- a flow mapping: `{cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}`.

Flow collections can be nested and may wrap over several lines; inside the brackets, indentation doesn't matter. Use them for short, simple values. Long or deeply nested data is easier to read in block style.

Inside square or curly brackets, the characters `,`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}` have a special meaning, so text containing them must be quoted there: `[a, "b,c"]`.

Flow style comes from **JSON**, another very common text format for data, used by most websites and apps to exchange information. JSON looks like flow style with every piece of text in double quotes: `{"name": "web", "ports": [80, 443]}`.

YAML 1.2 was designed so that nearly every JSON document is also valid YAML, with the same meaning. That's why tools that read YAML usually accept JSON files too, and why you can paste a piece of JSON into a YAML file as a value.

The reverse isn't true. YAML has features JSON lacks, such as comments, unquoted strings, multi-line text and anchors (reusable pieces, covered later). When YAML is converted to JSON, those are resolved or lost.

Block and flow styles produce identical data; the choice is only about how the file looks.
concepts.code:
# block style
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
resources:
  cpu: 500m            # to YAML, 500m and 1Gi are just strings
  memory: 1Gi

# the same data in flow style
ports2: [80, 443]
resources2: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}

# inside [ ] or { }, quote text containing commas or brackets
tags: [web, "env,prod", "[beta]"]

# a piece of JSON pasted in as a value is valid YAML
raw: {"id": 7, "labels": ["a", "b"], "ok": true}
takeaways: [a, b] and {k: v} are flow-style sequences and mappings
Block and flow styles describe exactly the same data
JSON is valid YAML 1.2; YAML adds comments, anchors and more
pitfalls: Leaving an unquoted comma in a value inside [ ], which splits it into two items.

options: Three items: a, b and c
quiz.explain: Inside a flow sequence a comma always separates items, with or without a space.

concepts.name: Multi-line strings: | and >
concepts.summary: Write long text with | (keeps every line break) or > (joins the lines), and control the final line break with - and +.
concepts.why: Lists of commands in automated build files, security certificates and long descriptions are all written this way.
concepts.body:
**Block scalars** hold text that runs over several lines, with no quotes or special codes needed. They start with `|` or `>` on the key's line, and the text is the indented lines below. Each line ends with a **line break** (or newline), the invisible character that starts a new line.

- **Literal** `|` keeps every line break exactly. Ideal for scripts (lists of commands), pieces of configuration and security certificates.
- **Folded** `>` joins lines with spaces, turning each blank line into a line break. Ideal for long prose that you want to wrap in the file.

Both keep the text's relative indentation. The indentation of the first content line is stripped from all lines.

**Chomping** controls the line breaks at the very end:

- default (clip): a single final newline;
- `|-` or `>-` (strip): no final newline;
- `|+` or `>+` (keep): all trailing newlines kept.

If the first line of content starts with spaces, give an explicit **indentation indicator**: `|2` means the content is indented two spaces relative to the parent.

In automated build systems (CI), `run: |` is how you write a step made of several **shell** commands, the commands you'd type in a terminal. Note that `>` doesn't fold lines that are indented further, which keeps indented examples inside folded text intact.

Inside block scalars nothing is special: `#`, `:`, quotes and backslashes are all ordinary text, which is exactly why they're convenient.
concepts.code:
script: |
  echo "building"
  make -j4
  # this is part of the string, not a YAML comment
description: >
  This long sentence is wrapped
  in the file but becomes one line.

  A blank line starts a new paragraph.
no_trailing_newline: |-
  value
keep_newlines: |+
  value

# parsed:
# script:  'echo "building"\nmake -j4\n# this is part of the string, not a YAML comment\n'
# description: 'This long sentence is wrapped in the file but becomes one line.\nA blank line starts a new paragraph.\n'
# no_trailing_newline: 'value'
# keep_newlines: 'value\n'   (plus any blank lines that followed)
takeaways: | keeps line breaks, > folds lines into spaces
Add - to remove the final line break, + to keep all trailing line breaks
Everything inside a block scalar is ordinary text, including #
pitfalls: Using > for a list of shell commands, which joins them into one line.

quiz.q: What string does this produce? key: |- followed by two indented lines a and b
quiz.explain: Literal style keeps the line break between lines, and the strip indicator removes the final newline.

concepts.name: Quoting: plain, single and double quotes
concepts.summary: Know when a string must be quoted, and the difference between single quotes (no escapes, '' for a quote) and double quotes (backslash escapes).
concepts.why: Unquoted special characters are the most common cause of YAML parse errors and wrong values.
concepts.body:
YAML has three **flow scalar** styles:

- **Plain** (unquoted): the most readable, no escapes, type is inferred.
- **Single-quoted** `'...'`: always a string, with no **escape sequences** at all (backslash codes such as `\n` for a new line). A single quote inside is written twice: `'it''s'`. Backslashes are ordinary characters, which makes single quotes ideal for **regular expressions** (text-search rules full of backslashes) and Windows file paths such as `C:\Users\ana`.
- **Double-quoted** `"..."`: always a string, with backslash escapes: `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\`, `\u00e9`, `\x41`. The only style that can hold any character, including invisible ones such as tabs.

Quote a string when it:

- would be read as another type: `"yes"`, `"1.0"`, `"null"`, `"0123"`, `"2026-10-17"`;
- starts with an indicator: `*`, `&`, `!`, `|`, `>`, `%`, `@`, a backtick, `[`, `{`, `-` followed by a space, `?` or `:` followed by a space, or a quote;
- contains `: ` (a colon then a space) or ` #` (a space then #);
- has leading or trailing spaces you want to keep.

A practical rule: prefer plain style for ordinary words, single quotes when something needs quoting, and double quotes only when you need an escape like `\n`.

Plain scalars can contain `:` and `#` when they aren't followed or preceded by a space: `http://example.com#top` is fine unquoted.
concepts.code:
plain: hello world
url: http://example.com/a#frag      # fine: no ": " and no " #"
title: 'Note: read this'            # must quote, contains ": "
comment: 'a # b'                    # unquoted, " #" would start a comment
pattern: '^\d+\.\d+$'               # single quotes: backslashes are literal
path: 'C:\Users\ana'
its: 'it''s'                        # -> it's
escaped: "tab\there\nnew line"      # double quotes: escapes processed
unicode: "caf\u00e9"                # -> café
alias_like: '*not-an-alias'
answer: 'yes'                       # string, not a YAML 1.1 boolean
takeaways: Single quotes: no escapes, '' for a quote; double quotes: backslash escapes
Quote values containing ': ' or ' #', or starting with * & ! | > % @ [ {
Quote values that look like numbers, booleans, null or dates
pitfalls: Writing a regular expression like \d+ in double quotes, where \d is not a valid escape sequence and the file fails to load.

quiz.q: Which value parses to the string He said "hi"?
quiz.explain: Inside single quotes double quotes are ordinary characters; the double-quoted version would need \" escapes.

concepts.name: Anchors, aliases and merge keys
concepts.summary: Define a piece once with &name and reuse it with *name, and copy one mapping into another with <<: to share default settings.
concepts.why: They remove copy-paste from big configuration files, such as automated build setups and Docker Compose files.
concepts.body:
A **YAML anchor**, `&name`, labels a value: any piece of the file, whether a scalar, a list or a mapping. An **alias**, `*name`, later in the same file reuses that same value. The parser fills it in, so the resulting data contains the value twice.

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  retries: 3
  timeout: 30
job_a: *defaults
```

To reuse a mapping but change or add some keys, many parsers support the **merge key** `<<`:

```yaml
job_b:
  <<: *defaults
  timeout: 60
```

`job_b` gets `retries: 3` and its own `timeout: 60`; explicit keys win over merged ones. `<<: [*a, *b]` copies in several; the earlier ones win.

Caveats:

- The merge key was defined for YAML 1.1 and is **not part of YAML 1.2**. PyYAML, ruamel.yaml, Go's yaml.v3 and js-yaml support it, but some parsers and tools don't.
- Anchors work only within one YAML document (usually one file; see the next lesson) and must be defined before use.
- Aliases are filled in when the file is read, so writing the data back out as YAML usually doesn't restore them.
- Tools like Docker Compose ignore top-level keys starting with `x-`, a convenient place to keep anchor definitions that aren't themselves config.
concepts.code:
x-defaults: &defaults          # x- keys are ignored by Docker Compose
  restart: unless-stopped
  logging:
    driver: json-file
  environment: &env
    TZ: UTC

services:
  api:
    <<: *defaults
    image: example/api:2.1
  worker:
    <<: *defaults
    image: example/worker:2.1
    restart: on-failure        # overrides the merged value
    environment: *env          # plain alias of a nested node

# worker parses to:
# {restart: on-failure, logging: {driver: json-file},
#  environment: {TZ: UTC}, image: example/worker:2.1}
takeaways: &name defines an anchor, *name reuses that node
<<: *anchor copies in a mapping's keys; keys written alongside it win
Merge keys are a YAML 1.1 feature, widely but not universally supported
pitfalls: Expecting an anchor defined in one document (or one file) to be available in another.

quiz.q: With base: &b {a: 1, b: 2} and c: {<<: *b, b: 3}, what is c?
quiz.explain: The << key supplies a and b, and the explicitly written key b: 3 wins.

concepts.name: Multiple documents in one file
concepts.summary: Put several YAML documents in one file with --- between them, optionally end one with ..., and read them all with a 'load all' function.
concepts.why: Kubernetes (a popular system for running apps across many servers) and other tools bundle several settings documents in one file this way.
concepts.body:
A YAML file, or more generally a **YAML stream** (whatever a parser reads in one go), can contain several **YAML documents**: complete, separate pieces of data. The lines that separate them are **document markers**. A line containing just `---` starts a new document; `...` optionally marks the end of one. The first `---` is optional.

```yaml
kind: Service
---
kind: Deployment
```

Each document is independent: it has its own top-level value, and anchors don't carry over between documents.

Most YAML **libraries** (ready-made code that programs use, here to read YAML) offer two ways to read: one for a single document, which **fails** if the file contains more, and one that returns all of them. In Python that's `yaml.safe_load` versus `yaml.safe_load_all`; in Go you call `Decode` repeatedly; Kubernetes' `kubectl apply -f` reads them all.

`---` also appears at the top of many files that have just one document, simply as a start marker. A **directive** such as `%YAML 1.2` may precede it to declare the version, though few files use one.

Typical uses: several Kubernetes settings documents in one file, a log that grows over time (`...` tells a reader an entry is complete), and **front matter**: a YAML document between `---` lines at the top of a **Markdown** file (a simple text format for formatted writing), holding its title, date and so on.

An empty document (two `---` lines one after the other) is read as null (`None` in Python), so skip those when going through the results.
concepts.code:
# k8s.yaml: two Kubernetes objects in one file
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
...

# Python:
#   import yaml
#   docs = list(yaml.safe_load_all(open("k8s.yaml")))
#   [d["kind"] for d in docs if d]      -> ['Service', 'Deployment']
#   yaml.safe_load(open("k8s.yaml"))    -> ComposerError: expected a single document
takeaways: --- separates documents in one stream; ... ends one
Use your YAML library's 'load all' function to read every document
Anchors don't cross document boundaries
pitfalls: Using the single-document function on a file with several documents, and getting an error.

quiz.q: A file has three documents separated by ---. What does PyYAML's safe_load do with it?
options: Raises an error because it expects a single document
quiz.explain: safe_load requires exactly one document; safe_load_all yields each one.

concepts.name: Implicit typing traps: the Norway problem
concepts.summary: Why NO, on, 012, 1:30 and 1e3 may not be what you think, how YAML 1.1 and 1.2 parsers differ, and how to stay safe.
concepts.why: Country codes turning into false and version numbers into floats are real production bugs.
concepts.body:
Implicit typing is convenient until a value that should be a string happens to look like something else. The infamous case is the **Norway problem**: in a list of country codes, Norway's code `NO` becomes the boolean `false`.

The rules depend on the YAML version the parser implements. Many popular parsers (PyYAML, older tools built on the libyaml library, Ruby's Psych, and Go programs still on yaml.v2) follow **YAML 1.1**, where:

- `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `y`, `n` and their capitalised forms are booleans;
- `012` is octal (base 8, so it means 10), `0b101` is base 2 (so 5), and `1_000` is 1000;
- `1:30` is a **sexagesimal** number (base 60, like minutes and seconds): 90;
- `2026-10-17` becomes a date value.

YAML 1.2's default rules for guessing types, its **core schema** (in YAML, a **schema** is a set of rules for deciding each value's type), are stricter: only `true`/`false` are booleans, octal needs `0o`, and sexagesimals and implicit dates are gone. Parsers following them include ruamel.yaml, Go's yaml.v3 (mostly), js-yaml 4 and the `yaml` library for JavaScript.

Some surprises exist in both: `1e3` is a float, `.5` is a float, `null` and `~` are null, and `3.10` is the float 3.1.

How to stay safe:

- **Quote** any string that could be read as something else: versions, codes, zip codes, times, IDs.
- Check the loaded data against a description of what it must contain (see the next lesson), so a wrong type causes a clear error.
- Know which YAML version your tool's parser implements.
concepts.code:
# key           YAML 1.1 (PyYAML)     YAML 1.2 core schema
country: NO     # False                'NO'
switch: on      # True                 'on'
answer: yes     # True                 'yes'
mode: 0755      # 493 (octal)          755
time: 1:30      # 90 (base 60)         '1:30'
date: 2026-10-17  # date(2026,10,17)   '2026-10-17' (ruamel.yaml still gives a date)
python: 3.10    # 3.1                  3.1
build: 1e3      # '1e3' (1.1 needs a dot) 1000.0

# safe in every parser:
country_q: "NO"
version_q: "3.10"
takeaways: YAML 1.1 parsers treat yes/no/on/off as booleans and 012 as octal
YAML 1.2 core only has true/false and 0o octal
Quote codes, versions, times and IDs; check types after loading
pitfalls: Assuming your parser follows YAML 1.2; PyYAML and many tools still implement 1.1.

quiz.q: With PyYAML, what does countries: [GB, NO, FR] load as?
quiz.explain: PyYAML implements YAML 1.1, where NO is a boolean.

concepts.name: Loading YAML safely in code
concepts.summary: Parse YAML with safe loaders (yaml.safe_load, not yaml.load with an unsafe Loader), cap how far aliases can grow, and understand round-trip loaders.
concepts.why: Some YAML readers can be told by the file itself to run code, so reading a stranger's YAML the wrong way lets them run programs on your computer.
concepts.body:
YAML can carry **tags**, labels starting with `!!` that tell the reading code (the **loader**) to create something other than plain data. For example, `!!python/object/apply:os.system` asks a Python loader to run a system command. A loader that obeys such tags runs whatever the file's author chose. So always use a **safe loader**, which builds only plain data:

- Python: use `yaml.safe_load` (or `yaml.load(s, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)`), never `yaml.load` with `Loader=yaml.Loader` or `UnsafeLoader` on files from people you don't fully trust. Since PyYAML 5.1, calling `yaml.load` without a `Loader` warns, and since 6.0 it is an error.
- Ruby: `YAML.safe_load`, the default for `YAML.load` since Psych 4.
- JavaScript: js-yaml 4 and the `yaml` library read only standard types by default.
- Java: SnakeYAML 2 is safe by default; older code calling `new Yaml()` was not.

Even safe loaders can be attacked with an **alias bomb** (nicknamed "billion laughs"): a few lines of aliases that refer to aliases that refer to aliases, so the data grows to billions of items once a program goes through it. Limit the size of the files you accept, and use a parser's limit on aliases where it has one (Go's yaml.v3 and the JavaScript `yaml` library do).

Some programs need to **edit** a YAML file while keeping its comments and layout. Normal loaders throw both away. Use a **round-trip loader** instead: **ruamel.yaml** in Python, the `yaml` library's `Document` type in JavaScript, yaml.v3's `Node` type in Go.

For speed in Python, `yaml.CSafeLoader` uses libyaml and is many times faster.
concepts.code:
import yaml

doc = '''
name: demo
ports: [80, 443]
'''
print(yaml.safe_load(doc))          # {'name': 'demo', 'ports': [80, 443]}

evil = "!!python/object/apply:os.system ['echo pwned']"
try:
    yaml.safe_load(evil)
except yaml.constructor.ConstructorError as e:
    print("refused:", e.problem)    # refused: could not determine a constructor for the tag ...

from ruamel.yaml import YAML        # round-trip: comments survive
import sys
rt = YAML()
data = rt.load("replicas: 2  # keep this comment\n")
data["replicas"] = 3
rt.dump(data, sys.stdout)           # replicas: 3  # keep this comment
takeaways: Use safe_load (or your language's safe function) for any YAML you didn't write yourself
Alias bombs can blow up memory even with safe loaders: cap input size
Use round-trip libraries like ruamel.yaml to edit files and keep comments
pitfalls: Loading user-supplied YAML with yaml.load(..., Loader=yaml.Loader) or UnsafeLoader.

quiz.q: Why is yaml.load(data, Loader=yaml.UnsafeLoader) dangerous on untrusted input?
options: Tags in the input can make it construct arbitrary Python objects and run code
quiz.explain: Python-specific tags let the document make the loader call functions such as os.system while reading.

concepts.name: Linting and schema validation
concepts.summary: Catch YAML mistakes early: yamllint for writing mistakes and style, JSON Schema for structure and types, in your editor and in automated builds.
concepts.why: Settings mistakes that a checker finds in seconds would otherwise show up as a failed release.
concepts.body:
Two kinds of checks catch most YAML problems.

**Linting** means running a checker, a **linter**, that looks for writing mistakes and style problems. `yamllint` reports uneven indentation, duplicate keys, spaces at line ends, overly long lines, values like `yes` and `on` that some parsers read as booleans (quote them or write `true`), and missing `---` document starts. Configure rules in `.yamllint`; the `relaxed` preset is a gentle start.

**Schema validation** checks the content against a **schema**, a description of what the data must look like: which keys are required, which values are allowed, number ranges, text formats. The most common kind is **JSON Schema**, a standard way to write such descriptions. It works on YAML too, once loaded, because YAML and JSON hold the same kinds of data.

- Editors: the **YAML language server**, a checking helper used by editors such as VS Code (through Red Hat's YAML add-on), checks files and suggests keys as you type. It picks a schema from the **SchemaStore** catalogue by file name (Docker Compose files and many others) or from a `# yaml-language-server: $schema=...` comment at the top of the file.
- Automated builds (CI): `check-jsonschema` checks files from the terminal; `kubeconform` checks Kubernetes files; `actionlint` checks the workflow files of one popular CI service.
- In your own program: read the file with a safe loader, then check the data with a JSON Schema library or a data-checking library such as Pydantic.

Duplicate keys deserve special mention: many parsers silently keep the last value, so a duplicated `image:` deep in a long file goes unnoticed. yamllint's `key-duplicates` rule catches it.
concepts.code:
# .yamllint
extends: default
rules:
  line-length: {max: 120}
  truthy: {allowed-values: ["true", "false"]}
  document-start: disable

# app.yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=./app.schema.json
name: web
replicas: two          # schema error: should be an integer
debug: yes             # yamllint: truthy value should be one of [true, false]
name: api              # yamllint: duplication of key "name" in mapping

# $ yamllint app.yaml
#   4:8   warning  truthy value should be one of [false, true]  (truthy)
#   5:1   error    duplication of key "name" in mapping  (key-duplicates)
# $ check-jsonschema --schemafile app.schema.json app.yaml   (once the duplicate is fixed)
#   app.yaml::$.replicas: 'two' is not of type 'integer'
takeaways: yamllint catches writing mistakes, style problems, yes/no-style values and duplicate keys
JSON Schema validates structure and types of the loaded data
Editors validate live via SchemaStore or a $schema comment
pitfalls: Relying on the parser to report duplicate keys; many keep the last one silently.

quiz.q: A manifest accidentally defines image: twice in one mapping. What do many parsers do?
options: Silently keep one value, often the last
quiz.explain: Duplicate keys are invalid per the spec but many parsers accept them; a linter catches them.

concepts.name: Tags and explicit types
concepts.summary: Use !!str, !!int and friends to force a type, understand local !tags used by tools like CloudFormation and Home Assistant, and how parsers map tags to types.
concepts.why: Tags explain both how to state a type explicitly and the custom additions many YAML-based tools invent.
concepts.body:
Every value in YAML has a **tag** that identifies its type. Usually the tag is resolved implicitly: plain `42` gets `tag:yaml.org,2002:int`. You can set it explicitly:

- **Standard tags** with the `!!` shorthand for `tag:yaml.org,2002:`: `!!str 123` is the string `"123"`, `!!float 1` is `1.0`, `!!int "7"`, `!!null`, `!!bool`. Also `!!map`, `!!seq`, and in YAML 1.1 `!!binary`, `!!timestamp`, `!!set`, `!!omap`.
- **Local tags** start with a single `!` and mean whatever the application decides. They are how tools extend YAML:
  - AWS CloudFormation: `!Ref MyBucket`, `!Sub "arn:aws:s3:::${Bucket}/*"`, `!GetAtt`.
  - Home Assistant: `!secret api_key`, `!include automations.yaml`.

A generic parser that doesn't know a local tag either errors or returns a placeholder. Loading a CloudFormation file (AWS's format for describing cloud setups) with plain `yaml.safe_load` fails on `!Ref`; you have to register a **constructor**, a function that builds the value, for each tag (or use the tool's own library such as `cfn-flip`).

Registering constructors is also how you map tags to your own types in code, the safe counterpart of the `!!python/...` tags: you choose exactly which tags are allowed and what they build.

`%TAG` directives can define your own prefixes, but they are rarely used outside the spec.
concepts.code:
import yaml

print(yaml.safe_load("a: !!str 123\nb: !!float 1\nc: 123"))
# {'a': '123', 'b': 1.0, 'c': 123}

template = '''
Resources:
  Bucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
Outputs:
  Name:
    Value: !Ref Bucket
'''
class Ref(str): pass

class CfnLoader(yaml.SafeLoader): pass
CfnLoader.add_constructor("!Ref", lambda loader, node: Ref(loader.construct_scalar(node)))

data = yaml.load(template, Loader=CfnLoader)
v = data["Outputs"]["Name"]["Value"]
print(type(v).__name__, v)          # Ref Bucket
# yaml.safe_load(template) -> ConstructorError: could not determine a constructor for the tag '!Ref'
takeaways: !!str, !!int, !!float force standard types
Single-! local tags are application-defined (CloudFormation !Ref, Home Assistant !secret)
Register a constructor per local tag on a safe loader to parse such files
pitfalls: Parsing a CloudFormation or Home Assistant file with a generic loader and getting unknown-tag errors.

quiz.explain: The explicit tag skips type resolution and keeps the scalar's text as a string.

concepts.name: Schemas: how plain scalars get their type
concepts.summary: Understand YAML's representation model: nodes, tags, and the failsafe, JSON and core schemas that resolve untagged scalars, and why parsers disagree.
concepts.why: This is the precise answer to every 'why did this value become a boolean/number/string?' question.
concepts.body:
YAML separates how a file is written from the data it means. Parsing produces a **representation graph**: the document's values (scalars, sequences, mappings), each with a tag. A plain scalar starts with the undecided tag `?`; quoted and block scalars get `!`. **Tag resolution** then assigns real tags according to a **schema**:

- **Failsafe schema**: only `!!map`, `!!seq` and `!!str`. Every scalar is a string. Safe and predictable; some tools and config loaders can be set to it.
- The spec's **JSON-based schema**: plain scalars must match JSON's own forms exactly: `true`, `false`, `null`, JSON numbers. Anything else is an error rather than a string.
- **Core schema** (the YAML 1.2 recommendation): the JSON-based schema plus friendlier forms: `True`/`TRUE`, `Null`, `~`, empty values, `0o` octal, `0x` hex, `.inf`, `.nan`. Everything unmatched is a string.

Only `!`-tagged scalars (quoted or block style) are **always strings**; that's the formal reason quoting works.

YAML 1.1 had no schemas in this sense, only a list of "language-independent types" with matching rules (regular expressions) that included `yes/no/on/off`, sexagesimals, dates and times, and the `<<` merge key. Most parsers' "default" behaviour is one of these rule sets, possibly with additions, which is why the same file loads differently across languages.

Many libraries let you choose: ruamel.yaml with `typ="safe"` and version `(1, 1)` or `(1, 2)`, the JavaScript `yaml` library's `schema:` option (`'core'`, `'json'`, `'failsafe'` or `'yaml-1.1'`), or Go's yaml.v3 when you read values into text (`string`) variables.
concepts.code:
from ruamel.yaml import YAML

doc = "a: yes\nb: 0o17\nc: 017\nd: ~\ne: '42'\nf: 1:30\n"

y12 = YAML(typ="safe")              # YAML 1.2 core schema
print(y12.load(doc))
# {'a': 'yes', 'b': 15, 'c': 17, 'd': None, 'e': '42', 'f': '1:30'}

y11 = YAML(typ="safe")
y11.version = (1, 1)                # YAML 1.1 resolution rules
print(y11.load(doc))
# {'a': True, 'b': '0o17', 'c': 15, 'd': None, 'e': '42', 'f': 90}

# JavaScript, npm "yaml" package:
#   YAML.parse("a: yes\nb: 1", { schema: "failsafe" })  -> { a: 'yes', b: '1' }
takeaways: Plain scalars are typed by the schema; quoted and block scalars are strings
Failsafe: all strings; JSON: strict JSON forms; core: JSON plus friendly forms
YAML 1.1 rules differ, which is why parsers disagree
pitfalls: Assuming two parsers agree on a file's types; check which schema each one applies.

quiz.q: Under the YAML 1.2 failsafe schema, what is the type of the plain scalar 42?
quiz.explain: The failsafe schema has only map, seq and str, so every scalar resolves to a string.

concepts.name: Edge cases: complex keys, indentation, gotchas
concepts.summary: The corners experts know: ? complex keys, non-string keys, indentation of block sequences, tabs, BOMs, long keys and string folding in plain scalars.
concepts.why: These details explain the odd parse results and errors that remain once you know the basics.
concepts.body:
A few corners of the spec that come up in practice:

- **Keys needn't be strings.** `1: one` has an integer key, `true: x` a boolean one (in YAML 1.1, `on:` becomes `True`, famously confusing PyYAML-based tools that read CI workflow files, where `on:` lists the events that start a run). Converting to JSON then turns the key into text, or fails.
- **Complex keys**: `? ` introduces an explicit key, which can be a sequence or mapping. Python can't use a list as a mapping key, so Python loaders may reject such documents.
- **Implicit keys** (without `?`) must fit on one line and are limited to 1024 characters.
- **Plain multi-line scalars** are allowed: a plain value may continue on more-indented lines, and the line breaks fold into spaces. This hides mistakes such as a forgotten `- ` that turns two list items into one string.
- **Indentation of sequences in mappings**: `key:` followed by `- item` starting at the same position is valid, because the `-` counts as indentation. But within one sequence all dashes must line up.
- **Tabs** are forbidden for indentation but allowed as separation inside lines and inside quoted strings.
- An invisible **byte order mark** (a marker some Windows editors put at the very start of a text file) is allowed only at the very start; the file must be saved as UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32, the standard ways of storing text.
- **Document markers in strings**: a line starting with `---` or `...` right at the start of the line, even inside a block scalar, ends the document; indent it.
- **Duplicate keys** are invalid by the spec even though many parsers accept them.
concepts.code:
1: one                 # integer key
on: push               # YAML 1.1 parsers: key is the boolean True
? [lat, lon]           # complex key: a sequence
: point
items:
- first
- second
  third                # not a new item: continues "second" -> 'second third'
message: |
  a line
  --- indented, so it is text, not a document marker

# PyYAML (YAML 1.1) loads the first two keys as 1 and True, and
# fails on the complex key: "found unhashable key"
takeaways: Keys can be numbers, booleans or even collections
Plain scalars can continue on indented lines, hiding missing dashes
Lines starting with --- or ... with no indentation end a document, even in a block scalar
pitfalls: Leaving out the - on a list item, so it silently becomes part of the previous item's string.

quiz.q:
In the YAML below, how many items does the list have?
- a
- b
  c
quiz.explain: The more-indented line c continues the plain scalar b, giving the items 'a' and 'b c'.
